newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 16.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--The International Monetary Fund delegation in Greece to evaluate the course of the economy has added its voice to the need for drastic changes to the job market as well as stressing the need for the creation of a strong supervisory system, following the deregulation of capital movement. The delegation is expected to hand over their initial report to National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou today.

--Greece appears determined to not allow imported secondhand cars to become cheaper despite indications from the European Court that it will rule in favour of the Commission on its suit against Greece. A ruling against Greece would mean the loss of state revenues from the special charge on imported secondhand cars. Deputy Finance Minister George Drys told Parliament yesterday that a special committee was looking into safeguarding public revenues and that the charges were imposed for environmental reasons. "Greece cannot agree to turn into a cemetery for used cars," he said.
--The commerce department is putting bills charged by mobile phone providers STET and Panfon under the microscope following complaints from subscribers over prices.
IMERISIA

--The capital market is expected to see new capital of about 685 billion drachmas in the first nine months of 1997. The amount includes the OTE - Greece's telecoms organisation - second share offer, estimated to reach 400 billion drachmas, as well as the National Bank's issue after the summer.

--Reliable sources say the IMF report on Greece is positive, with the greatest praise going to developments in inflation. The experts, however, have recommended to the government that public spending be contained and privatisations speeded up to contain deficits.

--The state, meanwhile, needs to see 40 billion drachmas coming into its coffers each day until the end of the month if it is to achieve the May goal of 850 billion drachmas, Deputy Finance Minister George Drys said.
KERDOS

--There's conflict and tension at the finance ministry between the customs services and the newly-established SDOE, economic crimes squad unit, charged with battling tax evasion on all fronts. Customs employees are reported to be angry at the SDOE intervening in their areas of jurisdiction and are reportedly undermining the new squad's work.
--The development ministry is planning a new bill that will effectively bolster existing law governing fair competition in the light of recent deregulations.
--The Bank of Greece is putting the final touches to new guidelines on calculating the volume of exports and levels of lending of Greek firms from foreign banks, to come into effect as of 1998.
NAFTEMBORIKI

--Procedures to draft the state budget for 1998 have already begun with a recent finance ministry circular advising the freezing of all primary public sector spending at 1997 levels, as part of the effort to contain state spending and reduce deficits.

--The state-run National and Commercial Banks have put an abrupt halt to the recent rate cuts, with National's governor Theodoros Karatzas advising calm and self-restraint before his meeting yesterday with Papandoniou. National is not expected to announce any rate cuts at its regular Friday meeting today.
--One of Athens' oldest retailers Akron Ilion Crystal closed yesterday due to overwhelming debts, including some 120 million drachmas to the Ionian Bank.
EXPRESS

--Greek banks can survive the intense compeition that the single currency will bring it only if they follow an aggressive mergers and cooperation policy, according to speakers at a seminar organised by the Association of Greek Banks yesterday.
--OTE yesterday approved Norwegian firm Telenor as its partner in Cosmote to develop the DCS-1800 mobile phone system.
--Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
